items.title: The most powerful communicators don't just perform. They connect.
items.quote: Bad Bunny stopped a sold-out stadium show to say something most of us forget. The bass was loud. Tens of thousands of fans were singing every word. He had the whole place in his hands. Then he stopped. And in that moment, he reminded me of something we teach every day: The most powerful communicators don't just perform. They connect. Here's what he said: ✅ "Don't forget to enjoy the simple things in life. The ones that seem small, but can be giants. Like dancing, like singing, like laughing." ✅

items.title: Pause before you speak
items.quote: 1/ Pause before you speak ↳ Not every point needs an immediate response. ↳ Give yourself room to translate your thoughts before broadcasting them.

items.title: Protect your core message
items.quote: 2/ Protect your core message ↳ Cut the unnecessary filler and over-justification. ↳ Being clear is better than being loud or verbose.

items.title: Listen for what isn't being said
items.quote: 3/ Listen for what isn't being said ↳ What people hear is filtered by their own context. ↳ Focus on how your message is landing, not just how it’s delivered.

items.title: Give yourself permission to say "Let me think about that"
items.quote: 4/ Give yourself permission to say "Let me think about that" ↳ A considered answer builds far more trust than a rushed one. ↳ Taking time to process shows respect for the conversation.

I remember standing just off stage, heart hammering against my ribs, I was convinced everyone was about to watch me fall apart. But I'd prepared. Obsessively. items.title: Skip the warm-up.
items.quote: 1️⃣ Skip the warm-up. ↳ Nobody needs three sentences of throat clearing before your point, lead with it.

items.title: Stop when you've landed it.
items.quote: 2️⃣ Stop when you've landed it. ↳ The moment you've made your point, close your mouth. Talking past it dilutes it.

items.title: Choose your words wisely.
items.quote: 3️⃣ Choose your words wisely. ↳Every extra one taxes your listener's attention.

items.title: Answer what was actually asked.
items.quote: 4️⃣ Answer what was actually asked. ↳ Not what you wish they'd asked. Give them the direct hit first.

items.title: Retire the corporate filler.
items.quote: 5️⃣ Retire the corporate filler. ↳ "Circle back," "synergistic alignment," nobody's impressed, they're just tuning out.

items.title: Trust the full stop.
items.quote: 6️⃣ Trust the full stop. ↳ A clean period carries more authority than a sentence that trails off.

items.title: Pick one takeaway.
items.quote: 7️⃣ Pick one takeaway. ↳ If they remember nothing else from this meeting, decide right now what that one thing is.

items.title: Speak in pictures.
items.quote: 8️⃣ Speak in pictures. ↳ A sharp analogy beats a paragraph of abstraction every time.

items.title: Listen more than you plan.
items.quote: 9️⃣ Listen more than you plan. ↳ The best communicators aren't rehearsing their next line, they're reading the room.

items.title: Let the pause sit.
items.quote: 🔟 Let the pause sit. ↳ Say the hard thing, then stop. Silence is authority.

items.title: 1. Pick your battles
items.quote: 1. Pick your battles ❌ Don't waste energy on every disagreement. ✅ Save your focus for what actually matters.

items.title: 2. Seek understanding
items.quote: 2. Seek understanding ❌ Don't focus on winning. ✅ Focus on moving the conversation forward.

items.title: 3. Deal with issues early
items.quote: 3. Deal with issues early ❌ Don't hope uncomfortable topics will disappear. ✅ Small conversations now prevent big confrontations later.

items.title: 4. Stay on the main point
items.quote: 4. Stay on the main point ❌ Don't argue over every single detail. ✅ Keep the conversation grounded in the big picture.

items.title: 5. Respond, don't react
items.quote: 5. Respond, don't react ❌ Don't feel forced to answer immediately in the heat of the moment. ✅ Pause, take a breath, and reply with intention.

items.title: 6. Set clear boundaries
items.quote: 6. Set clear boundaries ❌ Don't say yes just to avoid temporary discomfort. ✅ Respect your time and capacity as much as theirs.

items.title: 7. Let go of the last word
items.quote: 7. Let go of the last word ❌ Don't feel the need to prove you're right every time. ✅ Know when "enough has been said" and step back.

items.title: 8. Give solutions time
items.quote: 8. Give solutions time ❌ Don't force every issue to be solved today. ✅ Some conversations improve with space and processing time.

items.title: 9. Close the mental loop
items.quote: 9. Close the mental loop ❌ Don't replay the meeting in your head all evening. ✅ Accept that what was said is said, write down any next steps, and move on.

items.title: 10. Protect your energy
items.quote: 10. Protect your energy ❌ Don't expect clear communication when you're running on empty. ✅ Proper rest helps you respond calmly instead of reacting emotionally. The goal isn't to win every difficult conversation. It's to handle them well, and leave with your peace of mind intact. items.title: Stopping unnecessary apologies in the workplace
items.quote: The most overused word in the workplace isn't "busy." It's "Sorry." Early in my career, I said sorry a lot. "Sorry to bother you." "Sorry for asking." "Sorry, I don't know." One day, someone I respected pulled me aside. He said, "Why do you keep apologising?" I remember looking at him, completely confused. He continued, "You haven't done anything wrong." items.title: Prepare for their questions, not your script.
items.quote: 1️⃣ Prepare for their questions, not your script. ↳ The strongest presenters answer the audience's biggest concern before it's even asked.

items.title: Don't fight difficult questions.
items.quote: 2️⃣ Don't fight difficult questions. ↳ When someone pushes back, it usually means they're engaged. Treat it as the conversation you came to have.

items.title: Be comfortable with silence.
items.quote: 3️⃣ Be comfortable with silence. ↳ If the room goes quiet, don't panic and click to the next slide. Sometimes the best thing you can say is: "Can I ask what's giving you hesitation?"

items.title: Give 2–3 reasons 🏛️

items.title: Show the evidence 📊
items.quote: 3/ Show the evidence 📊 ↳ Use the data that proves your case. Not every piece of data you have.

items.title: Address the risks 🔍
items.quote: 4/ Address the risks 🔍 ↳ Show you’ve thought about what could go wrong.

items.quote: 6️⃣ Talk Like TED - Carmine Gallo ↳ Read this when you have a big presentation coming up and you want to hold the room not just get through your slides.

items.title: Steve Jobs ⏸️ : Pause
items.quote: 1/ Steve Jobs ⏸️ : Pause ↳ Silence shows confidence. When we're nervous, we tend to rush. A well timed pause says: I'm comfortable enough to let you wait.

items.title: Simon Sinek 🎯 : Start with why
items.quote: 2/ Simon Sinek 🎯 : Start with why ↳ Facts help people understand. Emotion gives them a reason to care. Start with why it matters before getting into the detail.

items.title: Barack Obama 📐 : Use the rule of three
items.quote: 3/ Barack Obama 📐 : Use the rule of three ↳ Three just works. It gives your message rhythm, makes it feel complete and helps people remember it.

items.title: Tony Robbins ⚡: Use your body
items.quote: 4/ Tony Robbins ⚡: Use your body ↳ Energy is contagious. If you look flat, you'll struggle to keep people engaged. How you show up physically changes how people experience what you say.

items.title: Jordan Peterson ⚖️ : Create contrast
items.quote: 5/ Jordan Peterson ⚖️ : Create contrast ↳ We understand things better when we have something to compare them with. Before vs after. This vs that. What happens if we act vs if we don't.

items.title: Mel Robbins 🪞 : Make people feel understood
items.quote: 6/ Mel Robbins 🪞 : Make people feel understood ↳ Before you try to change someone's mind, show them you understand where they're coming from. People are far more open to listening when they feel heard.

items.title: Jim Rohn ✂️ : Keep it simple
items.quote: 7/ Jim Rohn ✂️ : Keep it simple ↳ Knowing your subject doesn't mean telling people everything you know. The real skill is making something complicated easy to understand.

items.title: Dale Carnegie 🤝 : Make it about them
items.quote: 8/ Dale Carnegie 🤝 : Make it about them ↳ The best communicators don't spend the whole conversation proving how clever they are. They make the other person feel important.

items.title: Leave a decision
items.quote: 7. Leave a decision ↳ A clear ask: what she needed, and what the money would unlock. We gave people a way to understand why they mattered. You don’t need an extraordinary story. Think about a customer you’ve helped or a moment when you saw the problem for yourself. What happened? What was at stake? What changed? Say it out loud before you open your slides again. items.title: The compliment sandwich
items.quote: 1/ The compliment sandwich When you squish criticism between two compliments, people can start questioning the compliments too. ↳ Be clear about what you want to discuss and why it matters.

items.title: Venting instead of talking
items.quote: 2/ Venting instead of talking You’re still angry, and suddenly you’re unloading everything that’s annoyed you for six months. ↳ Give yourself time to cool down. Decide what actually needs addressing.

items.title: Guessing at motives
items.quote: 3/ Guessing at motives “You obviously don’t care” gives someone something to defend themselves against. ↳ Describe what happened and the effect it had. Ask for their perspective.

items.title: Waiting too long
items.quote: 4/ Waiting too long Something small becomes a pattern while you’re waiting for the right moment. ↳ Raise it while the example is still fresh.

items.title: Doing most of the talking
items.quote: 5/ Doing most of the talking You’ve prepared what to say so carefully that you forget to hear their side. ↳ Ask a question. Give them time to answer before jumping back in.

items.title: Leaving without agreeing on what happens next
items.quote: 6/ Leaving without agreeing on what happens next You think you’ve been clear. They leave with a different understanding. ↳ Agree on who will do what, and by when.

items.title: Softening it into nothing
items.quote: 7/ Softening it into nothing You say “maybe”, “a little” and “possibly” until the point disappears. ↳ Say the part you’ve been rehearsing in your head. Plainly and respectfully.

items.title: Launching straight in
items.quote: 8/ Launching straight in You’ve been thinking about this for days. They’re hearing it for the first time. ↳ Give them some context: “I’d like to talk about what happened in yesterday’s meeting.”

items.title: Letting updates take over the 1:1
items.quote: 9/ Letting updates take over the 1:1 You get through the task list and run out of time for the thing you needed to discuss. ↳ Make space for it at the start.

items.title: Never coming back to it
items.quote: 10/ Never coming back to it One conversation won’t always be enough. ↳ Send a short recap of what you agreed, then check in on how it’s going.

items.title: A quick acid test for your next pitch or presentation
items.quote: A quick acid test for your next pitch or presentation: If you woke up sick tomorrow, handed your deck to a colleague, and they could deliver your talk word-for-word, what would the audience miss by not having you there? In this clip from our latest PitchNinjas conversation with Terry Szuplat, we talked about something that’s easy to leave out of a pitch: yourself. items.title: Having starting phrases ready for difficult workplace conversations
items.quote: Have you ever left a conversation thinking, “I wish I’d said that differently"? Maybe you wanted to disagree in a meeting but didn’t know how to jump in. Or someone put you on the spot and you said yes, even though you needed more time to think. I’ve done both. Earlier in my career, I worried about sounding stupid, so I often stayed quiet. items.quote: I love moments like this. We worked with participants from Google.org Accelerator last year and one of our coaches Octavia Trenchard had the pleasure of working with Farhana Alarakhiya. She just forwarded me Farhana's talk below as it speaks to the work we do. This is the part I never get tired of. Seeing the effect of the coaching land on a real stage, in a real room, with a real person . 🎉 What I notice in Farhana’s talk: → A clear message, nothing extra → Pauses that let the big lines land →
